newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus parliament splits after referendum.
newsitem.headline: Belarus parliament splits after referendum.

text.p: Loyal supporters of President Alexander Lukashenko set up a new breakaway parliament in Belarus on Tuesday, formalising a split in the legislature over Sunday's referendum on extending his powers.

The split left the former Soviet republic with two rival parliaments, each claiming legitimacy. But the numbers and the political momentum appeared to be in Lukashenko's favour after his crushing victory in the vote, which critics said was fraudulent.

Deputies loyal to Lukashenko said 112 of the 199 members of the old parliament met behind closed doors in a building near the presidency and formed themselves into a "deputies' meeting" chaired by Yuri Malumov, a deputy speaker.
Between 50 and 70 members opposed to the president continued to sit in the main parliament building, but were unable to muster a quorum.
Lukashenko told his supporters they would form the lower house of his new two-chamber parliament, the "House of Representatives".
He claimed that 70.5 percent of the electorate backed him in the plebiscite, giving him a mandate to proceed directly with reshaping the country's institutions.
Political sources said the defection of a number of the president's opponents into his camp had given him the upper hand.
Lukashenko promised that all the former deputies, including those who did not get seats in the new 110-member lower house, would retain their status and perks as members of parliament.

Malumov, the most senior parliamentary official to cross over to Lukashenko's camp, said the deputies would meet again at four p.m. (1400 GMT) to cancel steps initiated by the old parliament to impeach the president.
Meanwhile the mood among the rump members of the old parliament was grim.
Speaker Semyon Sharetsky, acknowledging he was powerless to influence events, said: "We have the strongest force there is -- the moral right is on our side."
Sharetsky was encouraged by a statement from the U.S. State Department describing the referendum in Belarus as illegitimate, and by a visit from a delegation of the European Parliament.
Lukashenko's new legislature will also have an upper house or Senate, some of whose members he will appoint directly.
Lukashenko was in magnanimous mood on Tuesday, saying the losers in his country's political crisis should not be punished.
The United States on Monday said Lukashenko's victory was "deprived of legitimacy".

"We're quite disappointed that in Belarus yesterday the government went ahead with this referendum that has been labeled by the (Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe) and other international organisations as deprived of legitimacy," said State Department spokesman Glyn Davies.

Since winning the presidency by a landslide in July 1994, Lukashenko has become increasingly authoritarian, and he will now have powers that a Council of Europe analysis recently said "could not be stronger".
Parliament's draft constitution, which would have abolished the presidency and strengthened parliament, won the backing of just 7.9 percent of the electorate.
The electorate also voted overwhelmingly to keep the death penalty, let Lukashenko continue appointing local leaders and to keep a ban on the free sale and purchase of land.

Lukashenko has paid little regard to Western criticism and his main ally Russia signalled on Tuesday it was unlikely to interfere with his plans providing he manages to resolve the situation without violence.
Russia briefly intervened last week to broker a short-lived compromise between Lukashenko and his foes but the deal collapsed within hours, leaving the president a free hand.
President Boris Yeltsin's spokesman told journalists in Moscow on Tuesday the president expected all those involved to display restraint and preserve civil peace.
Yeltsin said he was aware that "a significant portion" of Belarussian voters supported Lukashenko in the referendum and believed Moscow's intervention had been crucial in lowering tensions.
